parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what must happen when the upward travelling sound wave reaches the top open end of the tube - can it just keep going as before?
Hint 2: Think about what happens when you now have two waves of the same frequency and wavelength travelling in opposite directions through each other in the tube.
parts.proper_answer: The incident wave is reflected at the top of the tube. The incident and reflected waves superpose to form a stationary wave.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reflection at the boundary**
You have one progressive wave travelling up. When it meets a boundary at the end of the tube, part of its energy is reflected back down. So now you have two progressive waves in the same air column, same frequency and wavelength, travelling in opposite directions.

Step 2: **Superposition into a stationary wave**
Where the two opposite waves overlap they interfere by the principle of superposition. At certain frequencies the interference produces fixed nodes and antinodes, so the wave pattern no longer travels. That is the stationary wave with antinodes A at the open ends and node N in the middle.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Start by marking on the h-axis where you know the antinodes A and the node N must be, using Fig. 5.1 and h measured from the bottom.
Hint 2: Remember amplitude is always positive, so the node means zero amplitude and the antinodes mean maximum amplitude joined by a smooth symmetric curve.
parts.proper_answer: Smooth symmetric curve with maximum amplitude at $h = 0$ and at $h = 0.60\text{ m}$, and zero/minimum amplitude at $h = 0.30\text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Locate nodes and antinodes on the h-axis**
Antinodes A are at both ends, so maximum vibration amplitude at $h = 0$ (bottom) and $h = 0.60\text{ m}$ (top). Node N is at the midpoint, so zero vibration amplitude at $h = 0.30\text{ m}$.

Step 2: **Sketch the amplitude shape**
Amplitude cannot be negative, so draw a U-shaped smooth curve starting high at $h=0$, falling to zero at $h=0.30\text{ m}$, then rising back to a maximum at $h=0.60\text{ m}$. It is symmetric about $h = 0.30\text{ m}$.

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about whether sound in air is transverse or longitudinal, and which way the incident wave is travelling in the tube.
parts.proper_answer: Vertical, along the length / axis of the tube.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the longitudinal model**
Sound is a longitudinal wave, so air particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer. The incident wave travels vertically up the tube, so particles oscillate vertically, along the axis of the tube. A stationary wave does not change this direction.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Check whether the two heights 0.10 m and 0.20 m lie on the same side of the node at 0.30 m or are separated by a node.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Same loop means same phase**
In a stationary wave all particles between two adjacent nodes vibrate in phase with each other. Both $h = 0.10\text{ m}$ and $h = 0.20\text{ m}$ are below the single node at $0.30\text{ m}$, so they are in the same loop. Hence phase difference is zero: $$\Delta \phi = 0^{\circ}$$

parts.label: (d)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 5.1: antinode to node to antinode over 0.60 m. How many wavelengths fit into the tube length for this first pattern?
Hint 2: Once you have the wavelength, think about which wave equation links speed, frequency and wavelength.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the wavelength from the tube length**
Antinode to antinode with one node in the middle is half a wavelength. So: $$L = \frac{\lambda}{2}$$ $$\lambda = 2L = 2 \times 0.60 = 1.20\text{ m}$$

Step 2: **Apply v = f lambda**
For sound, $$v = f\lambda$$ $$f = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{340}{1.20} \approx 2.8 \times 10^{2}\text{ Hz}$$ This is about $283\text{ Hz}$, given as $280\text{ Hz}$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (e)
hints: Hint 1: For a tube open at both ends, allowed patterns are $L = n\lambda/2$. You used $n=1$ in (d). What is the next integer $n$ as frequency increases?
parts.proper_answer: $f = 570\text{ Hz}$ (about $567\text{ Hz}$ to 3 s.f., double the (d) value).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Double the frequency for the next harmonic**
Open-open resonances occur at $$f_n = \frac{nv}{2L}$$ with $n = 1,2,3...$ Part (d) was $n=1$. The next stationary wave is $n=2$, where $L = \lambda$, so wavelength halves and frequency doubles: $$f_2 = 2f_1 = \frac{340}{0.60} \approx 5.7 \times 10^{2}\text{ Hz}$$
